nameStory: The American black currant gets its name from its dark purple-black berries that were prized by Native Americans and early settlers. The word 'currant' comes from the Greek city of Corinth, where small dried grapes called 'raisins of Corinth' were traded - early botanists thought these native berries looked similar to those Mediterranean fruits.
description: American black currant is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that grows 3-6 feet tall, forming loose, spreading colonies. It has distinctive maple-like leaves with three to five pointed lobes and produces drooping clusters of small yellowish flowers in spring. The flowers give way to smooth, dark purple-black berries in summer that have a sweet-tart flavor and strong, musky aroma.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three to five-lobed leaves shaped like small maple leaves, with toothed edges and a smooth texture. Crush a leaf and you'll smell a distinctive musky, almost skunky scent that's stronger than other currants.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, bell-shaped yellowish-white flowers hang in drooping clusters called racemes, usually with 6-15 flowers per cluster. Each flower has five petals and a sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Smooth, round berries about the size of a pea, turning from green to dark purple-black when ripe. They have a sweet-tart taste with a distinctive musky flavor and contain several small seeds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies through underground runners, creating patches of multiple stems. The shrub has smooth, thornless branches that arch gracefully outward.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and reddish-brown, becoming gray-brown with age. Unlike gooseberries in the same family, the stems are completely smooth without any thorns or prickles.

habitat: American black currant prefers moist, rich soils in partially shaded areas like woodland edges, stream banks, and swampy areas. In New England, look for it in deciduous and mixed forests, often growing alongside other moisture-loving shrubs like elderberry and spicebush. It's most common in northern New England but can be found scattered throughout the region in suitable habitats.

seasonality.spring: Drooping clusters of small yellowish flowers appear in May, filling the air with their sweet fragrance and attracting early pollinators like bees and flies.
seasonality.summer: Berries ripen from green to dark purple-black in July and August, becoming sweet and aromatic when fully ripe. Leaves remain green and lush in moist conditions.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, and any remaining berries become wrinkled but may persist on the bush.
seasonality.winter: Smooth, thornless stems with reddish-brown bark are visible, along with small pointed buds that help distinguish it from other Ribes species.

funFact: American black currant was once banned in many states because it can harbor white pine blister rust, a fungus that threatened the timber industry - but the shrub itself is completely unharmed by the disease and simply serves as an innocent go-between in the fungus's complex life cycle.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other currants in the Ribes family, but American black currant has the strongest musky scent when leaves are crushed. Remember: if it smells strongly funky and has no thorns, it's likely American black currant - gooseberries have thorns, and other currants have milder scents.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these native currants with the dried currants you find in baking - those are actually tiny grapes. Fresh currant berries from wild plants like this one are safe to eat and were an important food source for indigenous peoples, though they taste quite different from store-bought currants.
compareHints: Among New England's Ribes species, American black currant is distinguished by its strong musky leaf scent and completely smooth stems. Skunk currant has a similar smell but different leaf shape, while prickly gooseberry and smooth gooseberry both have thorns. Red currant has much milder-scented leaves and bright red berries, making American black currant the 'stinkiest' of the bunch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's currants and gooseberries, skunk currant is unique for its strong musky odor and preference for cooler, northern forests.
Among New England's Ribes species, prickly gooseberry is the most heavily armed with spines, making it easy to distinguish from the spineless currants like red currant or American black currant.
Unlike its gooseberry relatives in the Ribes genus, red currant has completely smooth, thornless stems and bears its fruit in long drooping clusters rather than scattered individual berries.
Among New England's Ribes species, swamp currant stands out for its incredibly dense coat of small prickles - no other currant or gooseberry in the region is quite so thoroughly armored.

Among its Ribes relatives, smooth gooseberry is distinguished by having fewer thorns than prickly gooseberry but more than the currants, and its berries grow individually rather than in the long clusters typical of red and black currants.
Unlike its spiny gooseberry relatives in the Ribes family, northern redcurrant is completely thornless and has a sprawling rather than upright growth habit.
European gooseberry has much more prominent three-pronged spines than our native prickly gooseberry or smooth gooseberry.
Appalachian gooseberry stands out from other Ribes species by its sweet berries and relatively smooth stems - unlike the very thorny prickly gooseberry or the skunky-smelling skunk currant.
Among the Ribes family, blackcurrant stands out for lacking thorns (unlike most gooseberries) and having that distinctive strong musky leaf scent.

Golden currant stands out among New England's Ribes species with its bright yellow flowers and sweet fragrance, while most relatives like skunk currant and American black currant have small, greenish or whitish flowers.
